title: Tu vs Tú: Your or You in Spanish?

body_html:
Tu vs tú is one of the first accent pairs Spanish learners meet. Tu without an accent is the possessive “your”: tu casa, tu madre. Tú with an accent is the subject pronoun “you”: Tú eres mi mejor amigo. They sound the same, so the accent is the only way a reader can tell them apart. The rule is simple, and one test will settle every doubt.

Quick answer
  • Tu = your (before a noun): tu libro, tus amigos.
  • Tú = you (subject): ¿Tú qué piensas?
  • Test: if you can add a noun after it, it’s tu.
  • After prepositions, “you” is ti (no accent): para ti.
{{toc}}

Tu vs tú: the core rule

TuTú
Meaningyouryou
Part of speechPossessive adjectiveSubject pronoun
Followed byA nounUsually a verb, or nothing
Pluraltusvosotros / ustedes
ExampleTu carro es rojo. Your car is red.Tú manejas. You drive.

The accent on tú is a tilde diacrítica, which the RAE’s guide to the written accent describes as a mark that distinguishes words spelled alike but with different functions.

Tu: your

  • ¿Cómo está tu familia? How’s your family?
  • Me encanta tu vestido. I love your dress.
  • Tus padres son muy simpáticos. Your parents are very nice.
  • Tu opinión me importa. Your opinion matters to me.

Tu is the informal possessive. With usted, use su: su familia. See {{link:tu-vs-usted|tú vs usted}}.

Tú: you

  • Tú tienes razón. You’re right.
  • ¿Y tú? And you?
  • ¡Tú puedes! You can do it!
  • Eres tú. It’s you.

Spanish often drops subject pronouns, so tú appears mainly for emphasis or contrast: Yo cocino y tú lavas los platos (I cook and you do the dishes).

{{image:2}}

Ti, contigo and te

After prepositions, “you” becomes ti, which never has an accent: Esto es para ti, Pienso en ti. With con, it becomes contigo: Quiero ir contigo. As an object pronoun, “you” is te: Te quiero. So the family is tú (subject), te (object), ti (after prepositions) and tu (your).

Other accent pairs that work the same way

No accentWith accent
mi (my)mí (me, after prepositions)
el (the)él (he)
si (if)sí (yes)
te (you, object)té (tea)

See {{link:si-vs-si|si vs sí}} and {{link:spanish-accent-marks|Spanish accent marks}}.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Why this is tricky for learners

In English, “you” and “your” look different, so there’s no visual confusion. In Spanish, the two words are spelled identically apart from the accent, and they sound the same. That’s why learners, and plenty of native speakers when texting, drop the accent. Usually context makes the meaning clear, but sometimes it doesn’t: Tu sabes might look like the start of “your knowledge…”. In anything formal, a missing accent here is one of the most visible spelling errors, a bit like writing “your welcome” in English.

A quick mental shortcut

Try adding a noun right after the word. If a noun fits, or is already there, it is tu: tu casa, tu idea. If a verb follows, or the word stands alone, it is tú: tú eres, ¿y tú?. Another trick: swap in mi or yo. If mi works (mi casa), write tu; if yo works (yo soy), write tú.

Real conversation

  • A: ¿Tú vienes a la cena de tu hermano? (Are you coming to your brother’s dinner?)
  • B: Sí, y tú traes tu guitarra, ¿sí? (Yes, and you bring your guitar, okay?)
  • A: Bueno, pero esta vez cantas tú. (Okay, but this time you sing.)

Regional notes

In Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America, vos replaces tú as the informal subject pronoun: Vos sos mi mejor amigo. The possessive stays tu: tu casa. So a speaker from Buenos Aires might say Vos y tu hermana, never vos y vos hermana. Wherever you are, the possessive tu never takes an accent.

The same logic applies to mi and mí: mi casa (my house) but para mí (for me). Unlike ti, mí does take an accent.

So remember the full set: tú, mí and sí have accents, but ti never does.

Try it yourself

  1. You are my sister. (Tú eres mi hermana.)
  2. Your idea is great. (Tu idea es genial.)
  3. This gift is for you. (Este regalo es para ti.)
  4. And you, what do you think? (¿Y tú qué piensas?)
  5. I love your friends. (Me encantan tus amigos.)

All pairs in {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Before a noun: tu. As the subject or standing alone: tú. After a preposition: ti, no accent. Get these right, and your messages will be clear to every reader.

faq.q: What is the difference between tu and tú?
faq.a: Tu (no accent) means your and goes before a noun. Tú (with accent) means you and is the subject pronoun.
No. Ti never has an accent: para ti, de ti, a ti.

faq.q: How can I tell whether to write tu or tú?
faq.a: If a noun follows, write tu (tu casa). If a verb follows or it stands alone, write tú (tú eres, ¿y tú?).
